questions.stem: A student investigates how the length of a nichrome wire affects its resistance, using the same wire diameter and temperature throughout. What is the dependent variable?
options: The temperature of the wire
The resistance of the wire
The length of the wire
The diameter of the wire
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the one measured in response to changes, here the resistance. Length is the independent variable that the student changes, and diameter and temperature are controlled variables kept constant.

questions.stem: A student plans to measure resistance at only three wire lengths, then changes the plan to eight lengths spread over a wider range. What is the main benefit?
options: The resistance of the wire no longer depends on its temperature
The trend between the variables can be identified with more confidence
Systematic errors in the ohmmeter readings are removed from the data
Each individual measurement becomes more accurate than it was before
questions.explanation: More data points over a wider range show the shape of the relationship more clearly and make a line of best fit more trustworthy. They do not remove systematic error or make any single reading more accurate.

questions.stem: Why should every measurement in a physics investigation be recorded with an uncertainty?
options: Uncertainty shows the difference between the measurement and the accepted value
An uncertainty is needed only when the result is to be compared with a theory
All measurements have limits to their precision, set by the instrument and method
Only measurements taken with analogue instruments need an uncertainty attached
questions.explanation: No measurement is exact: every instrument and technique limits how precisely a value can be known, so the result is stated as a range (±). The difference from an accepted value is error, which is a different idea from uncertainty.

questions.stem: What is the difference between precision and accuracy?
options: Precision applies only to digital instruments; accuracy applies only to analogue instruments
Precision is how close repeated results are to each other; accuracy is how close they are to the true value
Precision is how close results are to the true value; accuracy is how close repeated results are to each other
Precision is the number of decimal places shown; accuracy is the number of trials that were carried out
questions.explanation: Precise results agree closely with one another, while accurate results lie close to the true or accepted value. A set of results can be precise without being accurate, for example when a systematic error shifts every reading.

questions.stem: Five measurements of the speed of sound are 331, 332, 331, 332 and 331 m s⁻¹. The accepted value under the conditions is 346 m s⁻¹. How should the results be described?
options: Neither precise nor accurate
Precise but not accurate
Accurate but not precise
Both precise and accurate
questions.explanation: The readings are tightly grouped, so they are precise. They are all about 15 m s⁻¹ below the accepted value, so they are not accurate. This pattern points to a systematic error.

questions.stem: How does a systematic error affect a set of measurements?
options: It scatters the readings unpredictably above and below the true value
It affects only the first reading taken in each set of trials
It averages out to zero when many trials are taken and averaged
It shifts every reading in the same direction by a similar amount
questions.explanation: A systematic error, such as a badly calibrated instrument, pushes every measurement the same way, so it affects accuracy. Random errors scatter readings above and below the true value and do average out over many trials.

questions.stem: A student repeats a measurement ten times and averages the results. Which statement is correct?
options: Repeating reduces the effect of systematic error, but not of random error
Repeating removes both random and systematic error from the final result
Repeating has no effect on either random or systematic error in the result
Repeating reduces the effect of random error, but not of systematic error
questions.explanation: Random errors push readings both up and down, so they partly cancel when results are averaged. A systematic error shifts every reading the same way, so it survives averaging and must be removed by changing the method or calibrating the equipment.

questions.stem: An electronic balance reads 0.4 g with nothing on it, and the student does not notice. What type of error is this, and how should it be dealt with?
options: A systematic error; repeat each reading several times and average them
A systematic error; zero the balance before use or subtract 0.4 g from each reading
A random error; take more readings of each mass and average them
A random error; use a balance that displays more decimal places
questions.explanation: A zero error adds the same 0.4 g to every reading, so it is systematic. Averaging repeats cannot remove it, because every repeat carries the same offset. Taring the balance, or correcting each reading, removes it.

questions.stem: A student times a pendulum by hand, and the times for ten swings vary unpredictably between 15.2 s and 15.6 s. What is the main source of this variation?
options: Random error from the student's reaction time in starting and stopping
Systematic error from a stopwatch that runs consistently fast
Systematic error from measuring the pendulum's length incorrectly
Random error from the mass of the bob changing between trials
questions.explanation: Human reaction time varies from trial to trial, sometimes early and sometimes late, scattering the results: random error. A stopwatch running fast or a wrongly measured length would shift every result the same way, which is systematic error.

questions.stem: What is the difference between validity and reliability in an investigation?
options: Validity depends only on the number of trials; reliability depends only on the instruments used
Validity applies to the hypothesis; reliability applies to the conclusion drawn from the results
Validity is whether it measures what it claims to; reliability is whether results are consistent when repeated
Validity is whether results are consistent when repeated; reliability is whether it measures what it claims to
questions.explanation: A valid investigation is a fair test that measures what it is intended to, with other variables controlled. Reliable results are consistent when the investigation is repeated by the same or other people.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the drop height of a ball affects its bounce height, but uses a different ball for each height. How does this affect the investigation?
options: It has no effect, provided each height is still measured three times
It reduces validity, because a variable that should be controlled is changing
It reduces reliability only, because the results will not be repeated exactly
It improves validity, because more types of ball are included in the test
questions.explanation: The type of ball affects bounce height, so changing it means the test no longer isolates the effect of drop height. This uncontrolled variable makes the investigation invalid, and repeating trials does not fix it.

questions.stem: Three trials of the same measurement give 0.52 s, 0.71 s and 0.38 s. What does this mainly suggest about the results?
options: They have low validity, because the wrong variable was measured
They are highly accurate, because their average is a sensible value
They contain a systematic error, because each trial is different
They have low reliability, because repeated trials differ widely
questions.explanation: Widely different results for the same conditions are inconsistent, so reliability is low, usually because of large random errors. Inconsistency on its own does not show a systematic error, which would shift every trial the same way.

questions.stem: A student measures a length of 4.52 m and a time of 1.3 s. To an appropriate number of significant figures, what is the average speed?
options: 4 m s⁻¹
3.5 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: 4.52/1.3 = 3.477... When multiplying or dividing, the answer takes the least number of significant figures in the data. The time has two significant figures, so the speed is 3.5 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: A student adds masses of 12.36 g and 4.1 g. How should the total be recorded?
questions.explanation: When adding or subtracting, the answer takes the least number of decimal places in the data. The 4.1 g mass has one decimal place, so 16.46 g is rounded to 16.5 g.

questions.stem: How many amperes is a current of 250 mA?
questions.explanation: The prefix milli means 10⁻³, so 250 mA = 250 × 10⁻³ A = 0.250 A. Multiplying by 10³ instead gives 2.50 × 10⁵ A, which confuses milli with kilo.

questions.stem: Five measurements of a period are 2.31, 2.35, 2.28, 2.33 and 2.38 s. How should the mean be reported, using Δx̄ = ±(xmax − xmin)/2?
questions.explanation: The mean is 11.65/5 = 2.33 s. The uncertainty is half the range: (2.38 − 2.28)/2 = 0.05 s. Using the whole range gives ±0.10 s, which is twice the uncertainty.

questions.stem: A period is recorded as 2.33 ± 0.05 s. What is its percentage uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty/measurement × 100% = 0.05/2.33 × 100% ≈ 2.1%. Dividing the measurement by the uncertainty gives 47, and doubling the uncertainty first gives 4.3%.

questions.stem: A resistor is labelled 47 Ω with an uncertainty of 5%. What is its absolute uncertainty?
questions.explanation: The absolute uncertainty is 5% of 47 Ω: 0.05 × 47 = 2.35 Ω, about ± 2 Ω. Treating the 5 as ohms confuses a percentage with an absolute uncertainty.

questions.stem: Two lengths are 45.2 ± 0.1 cm and 30.5 ± 0.1 cm. What is their difference, with its uncertainty?
questions.explanation: When quantities are added or subtracted, their absolute uncertainties are added, even for a subtraction: 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 cm. Subtracting the uncertainties to get zero is a common mistake, and would claim an exact answer.

questions.stem: A resistor has a potential difference of 6.0 ± 0.1 V across it and a current of 0.50 ± 0.02 A through it. What is its resistance, with its uncertainty?
questions.explanation: R = V/I = 6.0/0.50 = 12 Ω. For division, percentage uncertainties are added: 0.1/6.0 = 1.7% and 0.02/0.50 = 4.0%, giving 5.7%. Then 5.7% of 12 Ω is about 0.7 Ω, so the result is written 12.0 ± 0.7 Ω, with the value and uncertainty to the same decimal place. Adding the absolute uncertainties gives ±0.1, which mixes different units.

questions.stem: The radius of a disc is measured as 2.0 ± 0.1 cm. What is the percentage uncertainty in its area, A = πr²?
questions.explanation: The percentage uncertainty in r is 0.1/2.0 × 100% = 5%. For a power, the percentage uncertainty is multiplied by the power, because r² = r × r adds 5% twice: 10%. The constant π has no uncertainty.

questions.stem: In finding kinetic energy, Ek = ½mv², the mass has a percentage uncertainty of 2% and the speed has 3%. What is the percentage uncertainty in Ek?
questions.explanation: The speed is squared, so its percentage uncertainty counts twice: 2 × 3% = 6%. Adding the 2% for mass gives 8%. Adding 2% and 3% once each gives 5%, which ignores the square. The ½ is exact.

questions.stem: A student's experiment gives g = 9.62 m s⁻². The accepted value is 9.80 m s⁻². What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation: Percentage error = |measured − true|/true × 100% = |9.62 − 9.80|/9.80 × 100% ≈ 1.8%. Dividing by the measured value instead gives 1.9%, and 98% is the measured value as a percentage of the true one.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a result's percentage uncertainty and its percentage error?
options: Uncertainty describes the spread of the measurements; error compares the result with an accepted value
Uncertainty compares the result with an accepted value; error describes the spread of the measurements
Uncertainty is caused only by systematic errors; error is caused only by random errors
Uncertainty can be calculated only with a theory; error needs no accepted value at all
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty comes from the measurements themselves, showing how precisely the value is known. Percentage error can be found only when there is a theoretical or accepted value, and shows how far the result is from it.

questions.stem: An experiment gives a value of g = 9.6 ± 0.3 m s⁻². The accepted value is 9.8 m s⁻². What can be concluded?
options: The result shows a systematic error of 0.3 m s⁻² in the method
The result agrees with the accepted value within its uncertainty
The result disagrees with the accepted value, so the method is invalid
The result is exact, because the uncertainty is less than 5%
questions.explanation: The result's range is 9.3 to 9.9 m s⁻², which includes 9.8 m s⁻², so the result is consistent with the accepted value. A difference smaller than the uncertainty cannot by itself show a systematic error.

questions.stem: Precise timing gives g = 9.62 ± 0.05 m s⁻². The accepted value is 9.80 m s⁻². What does this suggest?
options: A systematic error is likely, as 9.80 lies outside the range 9.57 to 9.67
Random error explains the gap, as 9.80 lies within the range 9.57 to 9.67
The result is accurate, as its percentage uncertainty is only about 0.5%
More trials will close the gap, as averaging removes all types of error
questions.explanation: The accepted value is well outside the result's uncertainty range, so the difference cannot be explained by random scatter alone. A systematic error, such as a mismeasured length or a timing offset, is likely. More trials reduce random error but not systematic error.

questions.stem: On a graph with uncertainty bars, the line of best fit has a gradient of 5.2, the steepest line through all the bars has a gradient of 5.6 and the least steep has 4.8. How is the gradient reported?
questions.explanation: The uncertainty in the gradient is half the difference between the maximum and minimum gradients: (5.6 − 4.8)/2 = 0.4. The value is the gradient of the line of best fit, 5.2. Using the full difference gives ±0.8.

questions.stem: A scatterplot with a linear trendline has R² = 0.99. What does this value tell you?
options: The data points lie very close to the linear trendline
The results are very close to the accepted value
There are no systematic errors in the measurements
The gradient of the trendline is equal to 0.99
questions.explanation: R² measures how well a trendline fits the data, with 1 meaning every point lies on the line. A high R² says nothing about accuracy: a systematic error shifts all points equally and leaves R² unchanged.

questions.stem: Data points plotted from an experiment lie on a clear curve, bending away from a straight trendline at both ends, yet the linear fit has R² = 0.95. What is the best conclusion?
options: The curve is caused by random error, so a straight line should be used
The R² value proves that the relationship is directly proportional
A linear model is not appropriate, despite the fairly high R² value
A linear model is appropriate, because R² is greater than 0.9
questions.explanation: A systematic pattern in the points, such as a curve, shows the relationship is not linear, even if R² is fairly high. A smooth curve is not random scatter. The data should be linearised or fitted with a suitable curve.

questions.stem: A student expects kinetic energy to be proportional to the square of speed. Which graph should give a straight line through the origin?
options: Ek against √v
Ek² against v
Ek against v²
Ek against v
questions.explanation: If Ek = ½mv², then Ek is directly proportional to v², so plotting Ek against v² linearises the data, giving a straight line through the origin with gradient ½m. Ek against v would be a curve.

questions.stem: A graph of kinetic energy (J) against speed squared (m² s⁻²) for a trolley is a straight line through the origin with a gradient of 0.25 kg. What is the trolley's mass?
options: 4.0 kg
questions.explanation: Since Ek = ½mv², the gradient of Ek against v² is ½m. So m = 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 kg. Taking the gradient as the mass gives 0.25 kg, and halving it gives 0.125 kg.

questions.stem: A student uses a line of best fit to predict a value well beyond the range of measured data. What is this called, and what is its main risk?
options: Extrapolation; the relationship may not continue beyond the data
Interpolation; the relationship may not hold between the data points
Extrapolation; it always increases the random error in the result
Interpolation; it can be done only when the line passes through zero
questions.explanation: Predicting outside the measured range is extrapolation. It assumes the relationship continues unchanged, which may not be true, for example when a resistor heats up at high currents. Interpolation predicts values within the range of the data.

questions.stem: Before a scientific paper is published in a journal, it usually undergoes peer review. What is the purpose of this?
options: The public votes on whether the conclusions should be accepted as true
The journal checks only that the paper follows its formatting rules
Other experts check the methods, analysis and conclusions for quality
The authors' colleagues repeat the experiment to get identical results
questions.explanation: In peer review, independent experts in the field scrutinise a paper's methods, data analysis and conclusions before it is published. This helps catch errors and unsupported claims, but it does not involve repeating the experiment.

questions.stem: A student needs an accepted value for the specific heat capacity of copper. Which source is most credible?
options: A social media post from a person who says they are an engineer
An advertisement for copper saucepans that states the value
An anonymous online forum where users discuss cooking methods
A physics data handbook from an established scientific publisher
questions.explanation: A data handbook from a reputable publisher is compiled from checked measurements and edited by experts. Social media, advertisements and anonymous forums may be inaccurate or biased, and their sources cannot be checked.

questions.stem: Why should a student acknowledge the sources of information used in an investigation report?
options: To show that the student's own results must be correct as well
To transfer responsibility for any errors to the original authors
To credit others' work and let readers check the original evidence
To make the report longer and appear more scientific to markers
questions.explanation: Referencing gives credit to the people whose work you used, avoids plagiarism, and lets readers find and evaluate the original evidence. Citing sources does not make your own results correct.

questions.stem: A class investigates the shielding of radiation using sealed low-activity radioactive sources. Which control best reduces the risk?
options: Placing sources close to the body so the readings are as large as possible
Handling sources with tongs and keeping the time spent near them short
Holding sources by hand, but only while wearing a cotton laboratory coat
Storing sources in a student's bag between lessons so they are not lost
questions.explanation: Exposure is reduced by increasing distance and limiting time, so sources are handled with tongs, used briefly and returned to shielded, locked storage. A laboratory coat does not stop gamma rays, and keeping sources close to the body increases exposure.

questions.stem: Why should raw data be recorded straight into a logbook during an investigation?
options: So there is an authentic, dated record of what was done and observed
So the data can be adjusted later to fit the expected relationship
So the final report does not need to include any of the raw data
So the investigation no longer needs a risk assessment beforehand
questions.explanation: A logbook is a continuous record of procedures, observations and measurements made at the time, which supports the authenticity of the results. Altering data to fit expectations would be unethical.
